answers.stem_only: Linux clients, NFS, concurrent shared read/write across two AZs, no app change, least overhead: Amazon EFS (Regional) with a mount target in each AZ, mounted on all instances.
Shared, persistent POSIX file storage for many concurrent VPC-connected Lambda functions: Amazon EFS with mount targets in the VPC (via an access point), configured as the function file system.
Shared NFS storage across AZs that grows and shrinks automatically with no capacity planning: Amazon EFS (elastic storage), mount target per AZ.

SQL Server FCI shared SMB storage across two AZs with low latency: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ with SSD storage joined to AD, and continuously available (CA) shares holding the data and log files.
Spiky, unpredictable throughput with burst credits exhausted: switch the EFS file system to Elastic throughput (pay for what is used).
Re-creatable data where loss of access during an AZ outage is acceptable, cheapest: EFS One Zone storage class in one AZ.
Windows clients, SMB with AD permissions, shared across two AZs, least overhead: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ joined to the AD domain.

Short-lived HPC needing very high throughput, data in S3, failure tolerable: FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the S3 bucket (data repository association), export results back to S3; no backups (scratch does not support them).
Steady, predictable throughput near peak all day with small stored data: switch EFS to Provisioned throughput at the needed level (cheaper than Elastic for sustained use).

ONTAP volume made via CLI gets the Snapshot-only tiering policy by default, so cold user data stays on SSD; set the tiering policy to Auto so cold user data and snapshots tier to the capacity pool while hot data stays on SSD.

Use EFS Replication to a destination file system in us-west-2 (RPO/RTO in minutes); at failover delete the replication configuration so the read-only replica becomes writeable and point the application at it.
Production data that must survive an AZ failure, cheapest: EFS Regional (Standard) file system with a mount target in each AZ; cross-Region replication is not required.
FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket (lazy loading of metadata and data on first access, so training starts at once), then export models back to S3.
Automatic AZ-level failover for FSx for Windows: move the shares to a Multi-AZ deployment (preferred and standby file servers in two AZs).
Lift and shift of NetApp ONTAP with multiprotocol NFS+SMB and SnapMirror tooling: Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP, migrate with SnapMirror.
One FSx for Windows file system has a maximum storage capacity well below 300 TiB, so use multiple FSx for Windows file systems grouped under one DFS Namespaces namespace for a single path.

Allow inbound NFS (TCP 2049) on the mount target security group from the on-premises CIDR only, and mount by mount target IP address (EFS DNS names do not resolve on premises without extra DNS setup).
EFS lifecycle management: transition to Infrequent Access after 30 days, and set the transition-out policy to move files back to Standard on first access (the default leaves them in IA).
FSx for Windows can join a self-managed (on-premises) AD domain directly over the network connection; no AWS Directory Service needed.
Make the report directory shared storage: mount an Amazon EFS file system (mount target per AZ) at that directory on every instance; no code change.
Database on an EBS gp3 volume (moderate steady I/O, cheapest SSD); shared uploads on one EFS file system with a mount target in each of the three AZs.
Amazon FSx for OpenZFS, which keeps ZFS snapshots and lets teams create writable clone volumes from snapshots, over NFS.
